In a serving engine, workloads are often unpredictable; a contiguous cache requires a single, massive block of memory to be allocated upfront. If the cache grows beyond this block, the engine must either fail or perform an expensive reallocation and copy operation to find a larger contiguous space. A paged cache, conversely, allocates memory in smaller, fixed-size chunks (pages) as needed. This allows the cache to grow dynamically without the risk of memory fragmentation or the latency spikes associated with moving large blocks of data, ensuring consistent performance even as the dataset expands.

When data is stored in fixed-size pages, the engine can predictably map keys to specific memory addresses using simple arithmetic (hashing to a page index), rather than traversing complex linked lists or searching through a massive, monolithic array. This predictability reduces the number of CPU cache misses (L1/L2/L3) because the processor can prefetch the relevant page more effectively. Additionally, paged caches handle eviction more gracefully; when memory pressure occurs, the engine can simply discard entire pages of cold data
